chapter_theme: Poems 41-60 are poems to the three crowns: Kovur Kizhar's interventions with Chola kings (omens before a march, a siege, a war between kinsmen, children before the elephant, a bard under suspicion), guide and praise poems for Chera kings, and Pandya poems that rank righteous rule above the army, liken the king to the gods and to sun and moon, and close with a Chola-Pandya alliance and a parasol mistaken for the moon. The recurring argument is restraint: poets use ancestry, shame and gain to hold kings back from cruelty and division.

41.reading: Death itself waits for its moment, but this Chola strikes whenever he wishes; in the lands of those who angered him every evil sign appears, in the sky, in the trees, in birdcalls and in dreams, and the people, dazed and defenceless, kiss their children and grieve with their wives in a great uproar.
41.nuance: The praise works entirely through the victims: a native list of portents (meteors in all eight directions, a leafless branch catching fire, teeth falling out, an oil bath and riding an elephant in dreams) makes the coming defeat look already decided, and the king is greater than Death because he does not wait. Several of the dream signs in lines 8 to 10 are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is about the enemy country awaiting the king's march, the matter of an invasion

comparisons.tenor: the king, who unlike Death does not wait for a fit time

42.reading: The Chola's elephants loom like hills, his army roars like the sea and his spears flash like lightning, so every king trembles; yet under his unbending sceptre his own fertile country hears no cry of war, only the noise of floods, and feeds guests from the dry lands; poets flow to him as rivers to the sea, while he turns on the land of the two rival kings with the force of angry Death.
42.nuance: The poem sets two kinds of பூசல் (clamour) against each other: inside the kingdom only the noise of rising water, never the cry of a raid; the peace within is the other face of the terror without. The catalogue of plenty (fish taken by reapers, tortoises turned up by the plough, honey from the cane, lilies plucked by water-carrying women) is offered as food for guests, so the land's wealth is measured by its hospitality. Line 18 recurs in poem 209, a formula for the watered country.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's excellence as ruler, his protection and might

comparisons.tenor: the country guarded by his sceptre
all the poets turning to the king
the king's might against rival kings

43.reading: The poet addresses a Chola prince of the line of the king who entered the scales to save a dove from a hawk: he admits he spoke in anger, asking whether hurting brahmins befits a son of such ancestors, and that the prince, instead of resenting it, was ashamed as if he himself had erred, showing that his house bears with those who wrong it; so the poet declares the fault his own and wishes the prince more years than the sands of the Kaveri.
43.nuance: The dove story is used twice: the poet invokes the ancestor's sacrifice for a weak bird to rebuke the prince, and the prince's forbearance turns the same family standard back on the poet, who ends with யானே பிழைத்தனென் (it is I who erred). The poem does not say what the quarrel was about; பார்ப்பார் நோவன in line 14 implies that the poet speaks as a brahmin who felt wronged.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the prince's excellence in forbearance and shame, a king's virtue

comparisons.tenor: the prince's shame at the poet's fault
the years the poet wishes the prince

44.reading: Inside the besieged fort the elephants, unbathed and unfed, rub against their posts and roar like thunder, babies cry for milk, women tie up hair without flowers and the houses cry out for water; it is bitter to sit here at ease: if you are righteous, open the gate saying it is theirs; if you are brave, open it with battle; being neither, to cower behind shut doors in a corner of the long wall is shameful.
44.nuance: The poet gives the besieged king exactly two honourable exits, yielding as an act of aram or fighting as an act of maram, and names the third, waiting behind the wall, as the shameful one. The suffering of elephants, infants and women is the argument: counsel here works by making the cost of delay visible.

thinai_evidence.note: the king addressed is holding a shut fort under siege, the defender's side of the siege

comparisons.tenor: the trumpeting of the starved elephant

45.reading: Neither of you wears the Chera's palmyra leaf or the Pandya's neem; both your garlands are of aar, so if either of you loses, it is your own house that loses, and both cannot win; this fight does not befit your clan, and it will only give deep delight to other kings like you with bannered chariots.
45.nuance: The argument is made through garlands, the emblems of the three houses: because both kings wear the same aar, the war can have no winner, only a losing house, and the only gain goes to dynasties outside. The appeal is to lineage and to the rivals' delight, not to compassion.

thinai_evidence.note: the matter is a battle between two kings of equal rank already joined; the colophon's thunai vanji names the poet's peacemaking

comparisons.tenor: the rival dynasties who will enjoy the Cholas' quarrel

46.reading: The poet reminds the Chola that he descends from the king who relieved the dove's distress and many others' troubles, and points to children of a house that shares its own food for fear of the hardship of those who live by learning; these small boys, who have stopped crying at the sight of the elephant, now stare bewildered at the assembly in a new distress; having heard this, the king may do as he wishes.
46.nuance: Two lineages are set face to face, the king's, famous for saving a dove, and the children's, famous for sharing with the learned; the verdict is left to the king, so cruelty would be a betrayal of his own ancestry. The children's having stopped crying at the elephant and now staring at the court shows a fear too young to understand what is happening. The syntax of lines 3 and 4 and the reading of line 8 (see source_issues) are not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem's act is a plea to a king, counsel on his own ancestry, not an invasion

comparisons.tenor: the protection a generous house gives the learned

47.reading: The bard's life of gifts, flying to patrons like birds, crossing wastes without counting them long, singing as well as an untrained tongue allows, rejoicing in what it gets, feeding its kin, spending without saving and giving without stint, troubled only about due honour, knows no harm to anyone; it walks with head high so that its rivals are shamed, and has a dignity like that of kings who rule the earth.
47.nuance: The poem answers a charge it never names: by insisting that the wandering bard harms no one, it lets us infer that a man who crosses frontiers from court to court could be suspected of serving the enemy. It then claims for the bard a pride equal to the king's, so the defence ends as a statement of rank.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the excellence of the bard's own calling (porul 2.16)

48.reading: Thondi of the seaside grove smells of honey from the garland on Kothai's chest, from the garlands of the women who embrace him and from the neytal flowers of the great backwater; that is our town and he is our lord; old-tongued suppliant, if you go to him, remember us too, and tell him: we saw the man whose fame rises whenever battle rises.
48.nuance: The pun on கோதை, the king's name and a garland, runs through the first two lines, so the king, his garland and the garlands of the women who embrace him all perfume one town. The request to be remembered turns the guide poem into a message the suppliant carries back to the patron.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem directs a suppliant to a patron, praise in the form of a guide poem

49.reading: Shall I call Kothai of the raised sword lord of the hills, lord of the towns, or lord of the cold shore where the sea roars? How can I name him, when the millet-watchers beat their rattles and the birds rise together from the nearby fields of bending ears and from the shining shore?
49.nuance: நாடன், ஊரன் and சேர்ப்பன் are the akam titles of the lords of hill, field and shore, and the answer is a single picture: one rattle in the millet patch lifts the birds of the paddy and of the shore at once, so the three landscapes lie close enough for one sound to cross them. Unlike 48, the poem gives no direction to a suppliant, so the colophon's guide-poem thurai fits it only by its pairing with 48.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is praise of the king through the extent of his land

50.reading: Before the blood-thirsty war drum, strapped tight and decked with peacock plumes, a garland of gems and golden uzhinai, had come back from its ritual bath, the poet unknowingly lay down on its soft couch, white as foam of oil; instead of cutting him in two with his sword, which would itself have proved that he knew all good Tamil, the king came near and fanned him with his drum-like arm, as if he had heard that only the famous have a dwelling in the higher world.
50.nuance: Two graces are graded: sparing the trespasser on the sacred drum would have been enough to show the king's learning in Tamil, but he went further and fanned the sleeper. The closing question explains the act by belief in fame as the passport to the higher world, so mercy is presented as the king's investment in his name.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises one gracious act of the king

51.reading: As nothing dams a flood, no shade shelters from overgrown fire and no strength stands against a gale, so nothing stands against angry Vazhuthi, who will not bear the claim that the cool Tamil land is shared; the kings who gave him tribute when he asked are free from fear, but pitiable are those who lost his favour, fluttering for a one-day life like the winged termites rising from the red mound the tiny termites built with toil.
51.nuance: 'தண் தமிழ் பொது' is quoted as a claim the king will not bear, that the Tamil land is common to the three crowns, so the poem praises a bid for sole rule. The termite image is double: the colony's long labour builds the mound, and the winged ones that leave it live a single day.

thinai_evidence.note: the king goes to war to take tribute from other kings, the matter of invasion

comparisons.tenor: the kings who lost his favour

52.reading: Like a strong male tiger that tires of its cave in the haunted peak, stretches with a groan and, driven by hunger, goes out to hunt where it pleases, Vazhuthi sets out to make the northern kings wither; if that is his aim, pitiable are those whose rich towns, where fish-smoke clings to creepers on the marutha trees, will turn to jungle, the common hall abandoned by its god and offerings, a forest fowl laying eggs in the dice holes the grey elders carved.
52.nuance: Praise is delivered as pity for the enemy: most of the poem pictures the after-state, the common hall emptied of its god and of its elders' game, with a jungle fowl nesting in the dice holes, so the king's glory is measured by the ruin it will make.

thinai_evidence.note: the king sets out against the northern kings, the matter of invasion

53.reading: To Poraiyan of the war elephants and swift horses, who ended the distress of Vilankil, the pearl-strewn town where bangled women play on the terraces of gem-bright mansions: your fame widens if spelled out and is still unfinished if summed up, beyond the grasp of bewildered minds like mine; yet in a world where the great were born one cannot refuse to sing, and since you wished that Kapilan of the flawless verse were alive today, I will sing your conquests as your rank deserves.
53.nuance: The poet measures himself against a famous predecessor whom the king himself named: the king's wish for Kapilar sets the standard, and the poet accepts it only by promising to sing to the measure of the king's rank. It is early evidence that a poet's name outlived him at court.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem's act is the poet's undertaking to praise, which is paadaan

54.reading: For suppliants like us it is easy to walk straight, as if we owned it, into the noisy old town where our lord sits and enter his court with heads high; but to the boastful kings who rose against Kothai, who gives without stint until the rain-cloud is ashamed, his land is like a wide tiger-haunted pasture that a herdsman with a leaf garland, grimy cloth and whistling lips will not approach with his small-headed flock.
54.nuance: The open gate of the court and the closed frontier of the land are made one fact: the ease with which bards walk in is the other side of the dread that keeps rival kings out. The herdsman with his leaf garland and grimy cloth is an everyday figure used to measure royal danger.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's giving and his dread among foes

comparisons.tenor: the king's land as enemy kings see it

55.reading: Maran, foremost among kings as the single eye shines on the forehead of the blue-throated god who strung the mountain bow with a snake and burned the three forts with one arrow: though elephants, horses, chariots and warriors make an army, a king's victory has the righteous way at its root; so do not bend the sceptre for your own or kill merit because it is another's; be like the sun in valour, the moon in gentleness and the rain-cloud in giving, so that the needy want nothing, and live longer than the sands the wind heaps at Senthil.
55.nuance: The four-limbed army is listed and then ranked below conduct, and conduct is defined as impartiality both ways: not bending the rod for 'ours', not destroying merit because it is 'theirs'. The three similes give the king one face for enemies, one for subjects and one for suppliants.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is counsel to a king (செவியறிவுறூஉ, porul 2.29)

comparisons.tenor: the years wished for the king

56.reading: Of the four gods who guard the world, the bull-bannered one with the axe and the dark throat, the conch-white one with the plough and palmyra banner, the sapphire-dark one with the bird banner and the peacock-bannered rider of the elephant, the Pandya equals the first in wrath, the second in strength, the third in fame and the fourth in achieving what he sets out to do; so let him give rare treasures to suppliants, drink cool Yavana wine poured in gold cups by bangled women, live happily, and endure with the world like the sun and the moon.
56.nuance: The likening to gods is systematic: four gods, each identified by banner, weapon and colour, each lending one quality. The counsel to enjoy life (இனிது ஒழுகுமதி) comes only after the command to give to suppliants, and the Yavana wine is a sign of foreign trade at a Pandya court.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king by likening him to the gods (பூவை நிலை)

comparisons.tenor: the white body of the plough-bearing god
the dark body of the bird-bannered god
the king's achieving what he intends

57.reading: Maran, whom all praisers, skilled or not, liken to Mayon: when you take another's land, let your young men plunder its fields of bending grain, let fire waste its wide towns, let your lightning-bright spear kill your foes if it will, but whatever you do, spare their guardian trees, for they will not serve as posts for your tall elephants.
57.nuance: The counsel allows plunder, burning and killing and draws its one line at the enemy's guardian tree, the emblem a house protects; the reason given is a practical irony, that such a tree makes no tethering post, which lets the poet restrain the king without preaching.

thinai_evidence.note: the counsel concerns the conduct of an invasion

58.reading: To the Chola, lord of the Kaveri and of Urandai, and the Pandya of Tamil Koodal, the young bull of the Panchavas who upheld his ancient house when the elders died as aerial roots hold up a banyan whose trunk has perished: standing together you shine like the white god of the palmyra banner and the blue god of the wheel; help each other, and if you never break your union the sea-girt earth will surely be yours; do not heed outsiders who, seeming good and kind and loyal to old ways, are eager to come between you; may your union stay as it is today, your spears rise in victory and other kings' hill-countries bear your tiger and carp on their peaks.
58.nuance: The address is balanced exactly, நீயே and இவனே twice, a line of praise for each, before the two are joined in one image of two gods standing together. The danger named is not war but go-betweens, described by three 'seeming' (போலவும்) phrases; the closing wish to carve tiger and carp together on others' hills makes the alliance a programme of conquest. Lines 6 and 7 (the young thunder and the snake) are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises two kings standing together and counsels them to stay so

comparisons.tenor: the young Pandya upholding his ancient house
the young Pandya who cannot bear old enemies

59.reading: Vazhuthi with the garland on your chest and arms that reach your knees, you are truly skilled at protecting with love and you know no falsehood; to your enemies you are like the sun that rises from the sea with unabating heat, to people like us you are like the moon.
59.nuance: The poem compresses the double simile of 55 into two lines, and the turn is in எம்மனோர்க்கே: the poet places himself among those who receive the moon's coolness.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is praise of the king's two faces

comparisons.tenor: the king toward his own people

60.reading: The poet and the virali, who had reached the edge of the wasteland like peahens, saw the full moon at the zenith, among twinkling red stars like a fishing boat's lamp in mid-sea, and hurried to worship it many times, because it looked like the white parasol of their lord Valavan of the true sword, a king like the strong ox that drags a salt cart's sunken wheel out of the rut on the road from the backwaters to the hill country.
60.nuance: The usual simile is reversed: the bards worship the moon because it resembles the king's parasol, not the other way round. The ox that hauls a salt cart out of a rut gives the king a working animal's image, strength shown when the load sinks.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's parasol, the sign of his protection

comparisons.tenor: the full moon among the stars
Valavan bearing the burden of rule

links.note: 41 opens 'காலனும் காலம் பார்க்கும்' (even Death watches for its time) to say the king does not wait; Naladiyar 36 tells the reader not to ask whether Death comes today or another day, for it stands right behind.
links.teaches: Both treat Death as an agent that chooses its hour, but the Purananuru makes that patience the measure a king exceeds, while the Naladiyar makes the unknown hour the reason for doing good now, so one belief about death supports a war boast in one book and a moral urgency in the other.

links.note: Kural 544: the world clings to the feet of the king who embraces his people and rules by the sceptre; 42: under his unbending sceptre the land knows no war cry, and all poets turn to him as rivers run to the sea.
links.teaches: The Kural states the reciprocity abstractly, while 42 shows what the embrace consists of (fields that feed guests, no raid-cry heard) and what the turning to the king looks like (poets flowing in like rivers), so the couplet's 'world at his feet' can be read as a picture of a watered, hospitable country.

links.note: Kural 1015 calls those who feel shame for another's fault as for their own the dwelling place of shame; in 43 the prince, wronged by the poet's words, is ashamed 'as if you had erred' (நீபிழைத் தாய்போல் நனிநா ணினையே).
links.teaches: The Kural's definition of the finest shame is acted out in 43 by a prince who blushes for the man who insulted him, and the poem adds the consequence the couplet omits: that shame shown this way disarms the offender, who then takes the fault on himself.

links.note: Kural 745 praises a fort that is hard to take, holds stored food and is easy for those inside to hold; 44 tells a besieged king that sitting secure behind shut gates and a long wall is shameful while his elephants starve and his people cry for milk and water. On the reading that both judge the king who holds out in a fort, they disagree.
links.teaches: The Kural values the fort as a means of holding out, while Kovur Kizhar sees the same holding out from inside, through starving beasts and infants, and calls it neither aram nor maram, so the pair shows the fort's strength and its moral cost as two views of one siege.

links.note: Kural 888: a house with inner enmity wears itself away like gold rubbed by a file; 45: two Cholas wearing the same aar garland fight, so whichever loses, their own house loses.
links.teaches: The Kural's file image says the house wears itself down, and 45 supplies the political arithmetic behind it, that between two branches of one house no outcome is a win and the only gain goes to rival dynasties, so the couplet's metaphor gets a concrete case and an outside beneficiary.

links.note: 45 warns two Cholas that their quarrel will give deep delight to other kings; Akananuru 346 closes on a Chola, Killi Valavan, worsted at Koodal and 'Kothai Marban's joy was great'.
links.teaches: An akam poet's closing allusion records exactly the outcome Kovur Kizhar predicted in puram, a rival Chera rejoicing at a Chola defeat, which shows that akam poets drew on the same remembered politics of the three crowns (whether this Killi Valavan is 45's Chola is not certain).

links.note: Both poems address Chola princes as descendants of the king who saved the dove (புறவு): 43 to rebuke a prince, 46 to stop the killing of children.
links.teaches: Placed together, the two poems show the dove story working as a family standard that poets could hold up to any Chola, in 43 to shame and in 46 to restrain, so the legend served as a check on royal conduct, not only as praise.

links.note: Kural 586 counsels the king to use spies who go in the guise of renunciants and wanderers; 47 insists that the bard's wandering life, crossing many wastes from patron to patron, harms no one. On the reading that 47 answers a suspicion of the wandering bard, the two disagree about whether such travellers should be trusted.
links.teaches: The Kural's advice to disguise spies as wanderers is the very reason a real wanderer could fall under suspicion, and 47 gives the wanderer's side, a life of gifts and honour that 'knows no harm to others', so the pair shows the cost the state's craft laid on the travelling poet.

links.note: 48 praises Thondi of the seaside grove, the Chera's town, as fragrant with the king's garland and the neytal of its backwater; Akananuru 60 likens the heroine's bright bangles to Thondi of Poraiyan of the strong chariot.
links.teaches: The same Chera port that a puram poet offers as his home and his king's glory becomes in an akam poem a measure of a girl's beauty, which shows that akam poets used a king's famous town as a byword for desirable wealth.

links.note: 49 asks how to name Kothai of the raised sword; Akananuru 346 ends on Kothai Marban rejoicing when a Chola was worsted at Koodal.
links.teaches: The Chera whom a puram poet praises as lord of three landscapes appears in akam as a rival who delights in a Chola defeat, which shows akam poets citing a living king's partisanship, not only his wealth, and lets the reader see the three-crown politics behind the praise (whether both name the same Kothai is not certain).

links.note: 50 says the king spared and fanned the poet as if he had heard that the higher world has a dwelling only for those with fame here; Kural 234 says that if one wins wide fame on earth the world of the gods does not honour the learned (or the gods) instead.
links.teaches: Both tie fame on earth to standing in the world beyond, and 50 shows the belief at work in a single act of royal mercy, while the Kural states it as a rule whose terms are disputed; the poem suggests that for a Sangam king fame was a practical reason for forbearance.

links.note: 51 and 52 are both poems to Maran Vazhuthi: 51 says the kings who resisted him are pitiable, living a day like winged termites; 52 shows what that pity means, their towns turning to jungle and their common hall abandoned.
links.teaches: Read in sequence, 51 gives the general verdict and 52 the landscape of its execution, so the reader sees how Sangam praise of a conqueror moved from a simile of brief life to a detailed picture of a deserted village.

links.note: Kural 1055: askers can stand before people because there are those on earth who do not hide what they have; 54: suppliants walk into the king's court 'as if they owned it' (உடையோர் போல), because he gives without stint.
links.teaches: The Kural explains why asking is possible at all, and 54 shows the confidence such a giver creates, a beggar entering a court with raised head; the poem also adds the other face the Kural omits, the same king's land as a tiger's ground to his rivals.

links.note: 55: though elephants, horses, chariots and warriors are excellent, a king's victory has the righteous way at its root; Kural 546: it is not the spear but the unbending sceptre that gives victory.
links.teaches: The Purananuru poet already ranks the four-limbed army below righteous rule before the Kural's couplet does, and he spells out the straight sceptre as impartiality toward one's own and others, so the Kural's maxim had a court-counsel form addressed to a named Pandya.

links.note: Kural 541 defines justice as acting after inquiry without favour to anyone; 55 asks the king not to bend the rod because a man is 'ours' and not to destroy merit because he is 'others'.
links.teaches: The Kural forbids favour in one direction only, while 55 names both failures, favouring one's own and injuring outsiders, so the poem shows that impartiality was understood as a double duty, protecting strangers' merit as well as resisting kin.

links.note: 55 asks the king to be like the sun in fierce valour and like the moon in cool gentleness; 59 says the king is like the sun to his enemies and the moon to people like the poet.
links.teaches: The same sun-and-moon pair is counsel in 55 and description in 59, so the anthology shows a stock image of kingship moving between what a king should be and what a poet says he already is, with the second poem naming whom each face is turned to.

links.note: 56 names the palmyra-bannered god and the sapphire-dark god among the four guardians of the world; 58 likens the allied Chola and Pandya to the two great gods, the milk-white one with the palmyra banner and the blue one with the wheel, standing together.
links.teaches: One poem divides the two gods among four to praise one king, the other pairs them to praise two allied kings, so the reader sees that poets chose a god-pair or a god-set to match the number and relation of the kings they praised.

links.note: 52 dwells on the enemy's land turned to jungle as the measure of the king's glory; 57 permits plunder, burning and killing in the enemy's land but asks the king to spare the guardian trees.
links.teaches: Set beside 52's relish of devastation, 57 shows that the same war poetry also drew a limit, and drew it at the sacred tree rather than at people, which tells us what the poets held more inviolable than the lives of the conquered.

links.note: 58 warns two allied kings against outsiders who come between them 'seeming good, seeming kind, seeming to follow the old ways'; Kural 826 says the words of the unreconciled, though they speak good things like friends, are soon seen through.
links.teaches: The Kural's general warning about feigned friendship is applied in 58 to an alliance of kings, where the danger is not the enemy's attack but his pleasant counsel, so the pair shows the couplet's subject was already a matter of statecraft.

links.note: 45 tells two quarrelling Cholas that their fight will delight other kings; 58 tells a Chola and a Pandya that if they never break their union the whole earth will be theirs.
links.teaches: The two poems state one calculation from opposite sides, division gives the gain to outsiders and union takes it from them, so together they show Sangam poets thinking of alliances between crowns in terms of who profits.

links.note: 60 likens Valavan to the strong ox that drags the salt cart's sunken wheel out of the rut on the road from the backwaters to the hill country; Akananuru 140 likens the speaker's suffering to that of the ox yoked to the father's salt cart sunk in deep mire.
links.teaches: The salt cart in the mire is a shared image of the coastal trade road, and the two books use opposite ends of it: the puram poet praises the king as the ox that frees the wheel, the akam speaker feels like the ox straining under it, so one working scene serves for strength in one and for heartache in the other.

new_concepts.gloss: the gift a bard seeks from a patron, and the life of asking for it
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word: பரிசில் வாழ்க்கை in 47 line 6

new_concepts.gloss: the guide poem, in which one performer directs another to a patron
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons of 48 and 49 (புலவராற்றுப் படை); 48 has the direction itself (அன்னோற் படர்தியாயின்)

source_issues: 42 line 18 is flagged as repeated in 209 line 6; it is a formula for the watered country, not a copying error.
43 line 5: 'ஏறுகுறித், தொரீஇத்' splits one word (ஏறுகுறித்தொரீஇ) with a stray comma.
46 line 8: 'கெட்டனை' (you are ruined) does not fit; probably a misprint for கேட்டனை (having heard); marked on the second reading and flagged uncertain.
47 line 4: 'மகழ்ந்தும்' is a misprint for மகிழ்ந்தும்.
48: show flags line 5 (அஃதுஎம் ஊரே; அவன்எம் இறைவன்) as absent from Duraisamy Pillai's edition, and the review's table says sangamtamil.com has a line 6 we lack; marked as it stands.
49 and 57: the review's table says sangamtamil.com lacks our opening line; in both, line 1 is integral (49's run of questions, 57's 'skilled or not' that line 2 completes), so all lines are marked.
